justifications.functional_suitability: Modular Monolith Core Scoring Engine handles scoring (R-01) with rule and ML modules. Case Management Service addresses analyst reviews (R-02). Zero-downtime updates are supported via atomic references (R-03). However, returning scoring decisions back through the call chain to Payment Gateway is not explicitly modeled.
justifications.performance_efficiency: In-memory evaluation using Java atomic references and fast validation pipeline helps achieve sub-50ms latency at 3,000 req/s. Asynchronous decoupling via Amazon SQS Message Bus keeps review handling off the critical path. Synchronous S3 Object Lock writes per request could potentially threaten the P99 budget.
justifications.compatibility: External interfaces use HTTPS/TLS 1.3 with Payment Gateway and Fraud Analysts. AWS API Gateway translates to gRPC/Protobuf. Although ML Training Environment is shown in context, concrete ingestion interfaces for model artifact delivery to the scoring container are omitted at lower levels.
justifications.usability: Fraud Analysts are served via Case Management Service and Case Review Controller over HTTPS. However, specific UI hosting or frontend interface components for human case operations are omitted, leaving user-facing interaction mechanisms implicit.
justifications.reliability: AWS API Gateway mentions circuit breakers, and SQS buffers spikes. However, the critical R-07 requirement (unblocking payments within 1 minute if scoring is unavailable) lacks an explicit fallback or fail-open mechanism in API Gateway or Fail-Fast Validation Pipeline.
justifications.security: Tokenization Proxy Container isolates PAN before passing data to the scoring engine, ensuring analysts never see raw card data (R-05). AWS S3 Object Lock and S3 Glacier enforce tamper-evident 7-year audit retention (R-06) compliant with PCI-DSS Level 1.
justifications.maintainability: Separation into Tokenization Proxy, Modular Monolith Core Scoring Engine, and Case Management Service provides clean boundaries. Configuration Validation Init Container prevents faulty deployments. A small team of three engineers can easily operate this cohesive, modular monolith structure.
justifications.portability: The design aligns with AWS eu-west-1 using ECS Fargate, S3, and SQS. Containerized microservices, gRPC, and standard Java facilitate modular portability, though deep reliance on proprietary services like S3 Object Lock introduces moderate cloud lock-in.

PERF-01.justification: In-memory evaluation using atomic references minimizes compute latency. However, writing audit logs synchronously to S3 Object Lock directly from the scoring engine introduces high I/O variance, threatening the P99 50 ms latency threshold under 3,000 requests per second.
sensitivity_points: Direct S3 Object Lock write latency on the critical path
tradeoffs: Immediate audit consistency versus maintaining strict sub-50 ms P99 decision latency

PERF-02.justification: Case management is fully decoupled from scoring via Amazon SQS. Analyst workloads query a dedicated Aurora Serverless read projection, preventing case screen queries from contending with real-time scoring workloads.
sensitivity_points: Asynchronous decoupling depth between scoring and case management databases
tradeoffs: Read projection eventual consistency versus complete resource isolation from scoring

AVAIL-01.justification: While API Gateway specifies a circuit breaker, no automated fallback engine, default rule execution, or offline audit persistence mechanism exists to render and record payment decisions when the scoring monolith crashes.
sensitivity_points: Absence of an explicit fallback decision strategy in the gateway or proxy
tradeoffs: System simplicity versus resilient automated fallback processing during engine outages

AVAIL-02.justification: The scoring engine writes directly to S3 Object Lock via the AWS SDK without an intermediate dead-letter queue or asynchronous local buffer. Any S3 degradation directly causes backpressure, stalling decisions or dropping audit records.
sensitivity_points: Synchronous coupling between real-time scoring and S3 write availability
tradeoffs: Simpler single-tier audit writes versus backpressure buffering during audit store outages

MOD-01.justification: The ML-Scoring Module explicitly implements Java atomic references for in-memory model hot-swapping. This architecture guarantees atomic pointer exchanges without downtime, rapid reversion within minutes, and explicit logging of the active model identifier.
sensitivity_points: Memory footprint when holding multiple model versions during atomic swapping
tradeoffs: In-memory model storage versus container memory limits under peak loads

MOD-02.justification: The Rule-Evaluation Module leverages atomic references and the Strategy Pattern for zero-downtime hot updates. However, the runtime distribution mechanism to push rule updates to active containers is unspecified, as the configuration validator is only an init container.
sensitivity_points: Dynamic configuration propagation mechanism across running ECS Fargate replicas
tradeoffs: Hot-swapping rules dynamically versus relying on immutable container redeployments

SEC-01.justification: Tokenization proxy ensures analysts and case management interact exclusively with tokenized data, preventing clear-text PAN access. Telemetry and traces are exported, but automated detection and alerting for anomalous analyst behavior within 15 minutes is not explicitly specified.
sensitivity_points: Isolation of PAN tokenization to prevent analyst exposure
tradeoffs: Strict boundary tokenization versus reliance on external SIEM for behavioral anomaly alerting

SEC-02.justification: S3 Object Lock enforces 7-year immutable, tamper-evident audit retention. Transition to S3 Glacier controls costs, and the asynchronous Restore Job Handler enables audit record retrieval within standard Glacier turnaround times well within one working day.
sensitivity_points: Glacier asynchronous retrieval latency profile for multi-year historical audits
tradeoffs: Lower long-term storage costs via Glacier versus asynchronous audit retrieval delay
